content: Post-travel depression, commonly referred to as PTD, is classified as an affective or mood disorder. Individuals experiencing PTD often report significant levels of depression upon returning from a vacation or a location that temporarily removed them from their usual daily routines. In the majority of cases, PTD is transient, and those affected typically return to their baseline emotional state over time, with the duration of recovery often correlating to the length of time spent away. PTD typically manifests after returning from a trip and attempting to reintegrate into a normal routine. The trips in question are usually positive experiences, and the depression arises from a sense of longing for the enjoyable moments that were experienced. Common symptoms of PTD include repeatedly looking at photos of the trip or the people and places missed, episodes of crying, loss of appetite, overeating, and other related behaviors. There are several approaches to managing PTD. The most common and effective treatment is simply the passage of time. A general guideline suggests that recovery may take approximately five times the number of days spent away. For instance, if an individual was on an eight-day trip, it might take around 12 days after returning to feel fully functional again. PTD tends to be most intense when returning from a particularly enjoyable or significant trip, such as coming back from a European vacation during the middle of summer break. Other strategies to alleviate PTD include surrounding oneself with positive influences, such as supportive friends or family members, who can provide emotional comfort and help ease the transition back to everyday life.
